warmup.q: Two app servers handle sign-ups for a wallet app. Each runs SELECT ... WHERE handle = 'ana', finds no row, then runs INSERT. The table has no unique index and PostgreSQL runs at its default isolation level. Two sign-ups for @ana arrive within a millisecond. What happens?
options: The second INSERT waits for the first to commit, then fails
Both INSERTs commit, and two users own @ana
The second SELECT sees the first INSERT and rejects the claim
PostgreSQL aborts one of them with a serialization error
warmup.why: Under read committed each SELECT sees only rows committed before it started, and neither insert has committed yet, so both checks pass. There is no row to lock, and without a unique index nothing makes the second INSERT wait. A serialization error needs SERIALIZABLE, and waiting then failing is what a unique index would give you. This lesson finds that one decider without a database.

sections.h: A uniqueness rule needs one decider for each value
sections.html:
Two people sign up for a wallet app within a millisecond of each other, and both ask for the handle @ana. Their requests reach two different app servers. Each server runs SELECT ... WHERE handle = 'ana', finds no row, and runs INSERT. Both commit. Two users now own @ana, and money sent to @ana goes to whichever row a query happens to find first.

The Transactions track's lesson on write skew and phantoms showed why. The check looks for a row that doesn't exist yet, so there is nothing to lock, and read committed lets both transactions through. Inside one database the fix is a unique index: every insert of 'ana' has to visit the same index entry, and the database makes the second insert wait for the first and then fail.

This track builds systems from logs and derived views, often across many machines. Take the database away and ask what the rule really needs. Two claims for the same handle must be decided by one decider, one after the other. If two deciders can each say yes without hearing from the other, sooner or later both will. That's why the Replication track's multi-leader setups can't enforce uniqueness: each region accepts its own @ana and finds the conflict later, after both users were told yes. Deciding which claim came first, for everyone, is agreeing on an order, and the Consistency and consensus track showed that agreeing on an order is consensus.

The simplest decider is one single-threaded process. It reads every claim from one log, in order, and keeps a table of taken handles. The first claim for @ana in the log wins, and every later one is rejected. It is correct, and every claim in the system waits in one queue. In this lesson's simulation, 2,000 claims through one partition had a p99 wait of 5,785 scheduler steps.

Claims for different handles never conflict, so they don't need the same decider. Split the log into partitions by a hash of the handle, the way the Messaging and logs track's producer lesson spread records by key. Every claim for @ana lands in the same partition, so one processor sees all of them in order and decides them alone, while claims for @bob are decided somewhere else at the same time. With 8 partitions the p99 wait fell to 2,274 steps, and no handle was granted twice. The client appends its claim with a request ID, lesson 3's operation ID made once per user intent, and waits for the answer that carries the same ID.

The partition key is the constraint. Route the same claims by user ID instead, and two claims for @ana from two users land in two partitions, with two processors and two tables, and both say yes. The simulation counted 937 extra owners that way, far worse than the check-then-insert race it was meant to replace.

try.title: Count duplicate handles in three designs
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. 2,000 users claim handles drawn from 200 popular ones, through three designs with the same seed.
Before it prints, predict: which designs grant a handle twice, and which one waits longest?
Look at the second table. What happens to the p99 wait as partitions are added, and why doesn't the duplicate count change?

Waits are counted in steps of the simulation's scheduler, so compare them with each other, not with milliseconds.

sections.h: A transfer is one logged request; the debit and credit are derived from it
sections.html:
A claim touches one partition. A transfer touches two. A user moves 8.00 from wallet w-03 to wallet w-12. With wallets partitioned by ID over 4 partitions, w-03 lives on partition 1 and w-12 on partition 3, and each partition's processor is the only thing allowed to change its wallets' balances. How do the debit and the credit happen together, with no transaction across the two?

The Transactions track's lesson on atomic commit answered with two-phase commit: a coordinator asks both sides to prepare, then tells both to commit. It works, at a price. Every participant must be up for every transaction, and a coordinator that dies at the wrong moment leaves both sides holding locks. A fault in one place becomes a stall everywhere.

Kleppmann, Beresford and Svingen's design for online event processing (CACM, 2019) makes one write atomic and derives the rest. Amounts here are in cents:

  1. The client makes a request ID, t-9, and appends one message, Requested(t-9, w-03 to w-12, 800), to the partition of the wallet the money leaves. That append is the atomic step: either the request is in the log or it isn't.
  2. Processor 1 reads it in log order. It checks that w-03 holds at least 800, takes the money out of w-03, writes Credit(t-9, w-12, 800) into partition 3, and answers Accepted. If the money isn't there, it answers Declined and writes nothing else.
  3. Processor 3 reads the credit and adds 800 to w-12, unless it has already applied a credit for t-9.

Now crash processor 1 just after step 2. It restarts from its last checkpoint and reads the same messages in the same order. Its state comes only from those messages, so it makes the same decision and writes the same Credit(t-9, ...) a second time. Processor 3 has seen t-9 and drops it. If the client times out and appends Requested(t-9) again, processor 1 finds t-9 among its decisions and repeats the answer without taking the money twice.

Four things make this safe: order within each partition, at-least-once delivery, processors whose decisions depend only on what they read, and one request ID carried from the client to the last write, lesson 3's operation ID.

Compare the design most teams start with. The API writes a debit to one partition and a credit to the other, two separate steps, and each consumer runs balance += delta on a table and commits its offset now and then. Nothing ties the two steps together, so they fail apart. The lab runs the same 1,000 transfers between 40 wallets, starting with 4,000.00 in the system, under the same faults: consumers that crash and apply again what they hadn't committed, clients that send twice, and an API that sometimes crashes between its two writes. The separate steps end with 10,456.00. 29 times the API crashed between its two writes and left a debit with no credit, 279 steps were applied twice after crashes, and 183 debit steps were refused for lack of funds with nothing to stop the credits written beside them. That last failure needs no fault at all: with every fault switched off, the two writes still end with 9,056.00, because the credit never hears that its debit was refused. The logged request ends with exactly 4,000.00. Take the request-ID checks out of it and replays alone push it to 8,474.00.

try.title: Count the money after crashes, in three designs
steps: Run the demo below from the labs folder. It sends the same 1,000 transfers through three designs under the same faults: consumers crash about once every 100 messages and replay, 5% of clients send their transfer twice, and in the first design the API sometimes crashes between its two writes.
Predict before it prints: which designs end with more money than they started with, which with less, and which with exactly 4,000.00?
Look at the run with no faults at all. Which line of runSeparateSteps makes it create money?
In the last two runs, compare credits sent with accepted transfers. Where do the extra credits come from, and why don't they matter in the last run?

code.html: // separate steps: two writes, then balance += delta, with no id to recognise a repeat logs[part(t.from)] += Step(t.requestId, t.from, -t.amount) // write 1: the debit logs[part(t.to)] += Step(t.requestId, t.to, t.amount) // write 2: the credit // one logged request: the destination drops a credit it has already applied is Credit -> { if (!creditsApplied.add(msg.requestId) && dedupe) return // seen this credit: drop the duplicate balances[msg.wallet] = balances.getValue(msg.wallet) + msg.amount }

-- debit and credit as two separate writes, applied with balance += delta
   half-written transfers 29, debits refused on their own 183, steps applied twice 279
   money in the system: 1045600 (should be 400000, off by 645600)
-- the same two writes with no faults at all
   debits refused on their own 122
   money in the system: 905600 (should be 400000, off by 505600)
-- one logged request, debit and credit derived from it, request ids not checked
   crashes 25, credits sent 985 for 787 accepted transfers
   money in the system: 847400 (should be 400000, off by 447400)
-- one logged request, debit and credit derived from it, request ids checked
   crashes 22, credits sent 854 for 764 accepted transfers
   money in the system: 400000 (should be 400000, off by 0)

Amounts are in cents. The separate writes create money even with no faults: a debit refused for lack of funds can't stop a credit that was written separately. With faults, half-written transfers lose money and steps applied twice move it both ways, and the total is off by 6,456.00. The logged request decides once, at the source, so a refused transfer never produces a credit. Every replay after a crash still sends some credits again, which is why both of its runs send more credits than they accept transfers. Without the request-ID check each duplicate is added again; with it, the duplicates are dropped and the total is exact. The runs accept slightly different numbers of transfers because crashes change the order in which credits and requests meet.

sections.h: Timeliness and integrity are two different promises
sections.html:
Every design in the transfer demo has the same delay built in. A credit reaches the recipient's partition some time after the debit, so for a moment the money is in neither wallet, and anyone who looks at the recipient then sees the old balance. The correct design is as slow as the broken ones in that sense. What separated them is what was left at the end.

The word "consistency" usually lumps together two different properties.

Timeliness means users see state that is up to date. A violation is a stale read: the credit hasn't arrived, the dashboard is 30 seconds behind. Wait, and it goes away. Linearizability, from the Consistency and consensus track, is the strongest form of it, and read-your-writes is a weaker one.

Integrity means nothing is lost, nothing is invented, and nothing contradicts anything else: every derived view says what the log says. A violation is permanent. A credit applied twice stays applied twice until someone finds it and writes a correction, and waiting doesn't help.

Think of a merchant's dashboard. If today's sales figure trails real time by a minute, nobody calls support. If the payout file says 1,208.40 and the ledger says 1,200.40, that's an incident, and every later payout built on that ledger inherits the 8.00. In almost every system that holds money or records about people, integrity matters far more than timeliness. "Eventually consistent" is a fair promise about timeliness. It is never an excuse for an integrity bug.

An ACID transaction gives you both at once, which is why few people bother to tell them apart. The log design pulls them apart. Integrity comes from the single atomic append, decisions derived only from the log, the request ID carried end to end, and an immutable log you can replay to check and repair derived state (lesson 5 builds that audit). None of these needs a client to wait. Timeliness you buy only where a user needs it, with lesson 2's wait for your own write's offset, which took that lab's stale reads from 331 in 1,000 to none. Most reads don't need it, so most reads don't pay for it.

try.title: Sort six incidents into timeliness and integrity
steps: For each incident, decide: timeliness (fixes itself if you wait) or integrity (stays wrong until someone repairs it)?

1. A refund appears on the merchant dashboard 40 seconds after the API returned. 2. A consumer redelivered 12 ledger postings after a rebalance and added them again. 3. The search index still finds a payment link cancelled two seconds ago. 4. A settlement file's total differs from the sum of the payments it lists. 5. For a few seconds after a claim, one phone shows @ana as yours and another shows it as free. 6. A projection hit a record it couldn't deserialize, logged a warning and moved on.
For each integrity one, write down what would detect it.
try.expect:
Timeliness: 1, 3 and 5. Each is a view that hasn't caught up yet, and each fixes itself once the change propagates; if the user can't tolerate the wait, have them wait for their own write.

Integrity: 2, 4 and 6. The 12 postings stay doubled, the settlement file stays wrong, and the skipped record stays missing from the projection, however long you wait. Detection: recompute the projection from the log and diff it against the live one, reconcile the file's total against the ledger before it is sent, and treat a record you can't read as a stop-the-line error rather than a warning. Lesson 5 builds the recompute-and-diff audit.

sections.h: Many rules can be checked late and repaired with an apology
sections.html:
Uniqueness forced every claim for one handle through one decider. Most business rules are gentler, and businesses broke them long before computers did. An airline sells more seats than the plane has, because some passengers don't show up, and when they all do, it pays the extra ones to take a later flight. A shop sells its last kettle twice and emails one customer an apology and a voucher. A bank lets an account go overdrawn and charges a fee. In each case the rule is checked late, and a violation is repaired with a compensating action, the saga step from the Transactions track's lesson on atomic commit, often run by people.

Pat Helland and Dave Campbell put it in one line in "Building on Quicksand" (CIDR 2009): computing is memories, guesses and apologies. A node acts on what it knows locally, so each action is a guess, and when a guess turns out wrong, the business apologizes. Their example rule is "don't overbook the airplane by more than 15%". Whether to coordinate becomes a business question: what does an apology cost, and what does waiting for coordination cost? Write optimistically and check afterwards where apologies are cheap. Check synchronously before anything you can't take back, such as sending money to a card network or a bank. Integrity still holds everywhere: an overbooked seat is a known, recorded state with a process attached, and a lost booking is not.

Peter Bailis and colleagues made "when must you coordinate" precise ("Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems", PVLDB 2014). A rule is invariant confluent if two replicas can start from the same valid state, accept different transactions on their own, and always merge into a state that is still valid. Such a rule needs no coordination at all. Their table settles the common cases:

Rule, and the operation Coordination needed?
NOT NULL or a value check, any write no
foreign key, insert no
foreign key, delete yes
unique value the user chooses (@ana) yes
unique value the system chooses (each node has its own ID range) no
AUTO_INCREMENT, IDs in sequence yes
counter with a lower bound, increment no
counter with a lower bound, decrement (a balance that must stay above zero) yes

Their prototype ran the TPC-C New-Order benchmark, coordinating only where the analysis said it must, at 12.7 million transactions a second on 200 servers, 25 times the best result published before.

A year later the same group looked at what applications actually do ("Feral Concurrency Control", SIGMOD 2015). Across 67 open-source Rails applications, models declared on average 1.80 validations each, against 0.13 transactions and 0.01 locks. Rails' uniqueness validation is check-then-insert at the database's default isolation. The authors sent 64 concurrent requests with the same key, for 100 rounds. Without the validation, all 6,300 duplicates went in. With it, 70 got through when two Rails processes raced, and more with more processes, staying just under 700. With a unique index in the database, none did. Uniqueness is not invariant confluent, and checking it in the application doesn't change that. Put the decision in one place: a unique index, or one partition of a log.

try.title: Which payment rules need coordination?
steps: Imagine the payments service runs in two regions that accept writes on their own. For each rule, decide whether the two regions could each check it locally and still be right after their changes merge.

(a) A payment's amount is positive. (b) Every payment references an existing merchant, checked when the payment is inserted. (c) A merchant can be deleted only if no payment references it. (d) An idempotency key, chosen by the client, is unique per merchant. (e) Payout IDs are unique, generated by the server. (f) A wallet balance never goes below zero. (g) A merchant's payouts add up to at most 10,000.00 a day.
For each rule that needs coordination, name the cheapest thing that would do: one partition, a unique index, or an apology.
try.expect:
No coordination: (a) is a check on one row; (b) is a foreign-key insert, and merging two sets of valid payments can't make a merchant disappear; (e) works if each region generates IDs from its own range or with its own prefix.

Coordination: (c) is a foreign-key delete: one region deletes the merchant while the other inserts a payment for it. (d) is a unique value the user chooses: route every request for a (merchant, key) pair to one partition, or put a unique index on it in one database. (f) and (g) are counters with a bound, decremented by withdrawals and payouts: two regions each spend the last 50.00. Either route all of one wallet's or merchant's withdrawals to one partition, which the transfer design already does, or split the budget (5,000.00 per region per day) and let a region that runs out ask the other. A business may also choose to allow a small overdraft and apologize with a fee, which is (f) checked late on purpose.

refs.title: Bailis et al., Coordination Avoidance in Database Systems (PVLDB, 2014)
Bailis et al., Feral Concurrency Control (SIGMOD, 2015)
Helland and Campbell, Building on Quicksand (CIDR, 2009)

analogy: A theatre box office for one night's show. Ticket requests arrive through many sellers, but every request for a given night goes to the one clerk who holds that night's seating chart, and the clerk handles them one at a time: the first request for seat F12 gets it, the second is told no. Other nights have other clerks, so the office grows by nights, not by seats. Route requests by the buyer's surname instead of by night, and two clerks with two copies of the chart sell F12 twice. When the theatre deliberately sells a few more standing tickets than it has room for, it keeps vouchers ready for the evening someone can't get in. The analogy breaks at recovery. A clerk who faints still has every decision written in the chart, while a processor that crashes loses its memory, and gets it back only because it can replay the log and make the same decisions in the same order.
world: Much of this design is already in a payments stack. An idempotency key must be unique per merchant, so key the topic or the table by (merchant, key), never by payment ID. A ledger topic keyed by account ID makes one consumer per partition the only writer of each account's balance; a Kafka Streams processor with a state store does what this lesson's WalletProcessor does, and its changelog topic plays the checkpoint. A transfer between accounts in different partitions becomes one request record plus derived debit and credit records, each carrying the request ID and deduplicated at its consumer, instead of an XA transaction across two Oracle schemas. Temporal gives you a decider for free: it allows only one open workflow execution per workflow ID in a namespace, so a workflow ID made from the request ID is a uniqueness constraint. And card payments run on guesses and apologies: an authorization is a guess, refunds, reversals and chargebacks are the apologies, and integrity comes from settlement files that must reconcile to the cent.
mistake: Enforcing uniqueness in application code: an ORM validation, existsByHandle() followed by save(), or a cache lookup before a write. People do it because it reads exactly like the rule and passes every test that sends one request at a time. Under concurrency it is check-then-insert, and the Feral Concurrency Control study counted the duplicates it lets through. The second form of the mistake is partitioning by the wrong key: a topic keyed by customer ID when the rule is about the handle, or by payment ID when the rule is about the idempotency key. Fix both by putting the decision where all conflicting writes meet: a unique index (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, then check the row count), or a log partitioned by exactly the value the rule is about.

compare.title: Check-then-insert, and a log that decides

a.label: Check-then-insert
a.title: on each of 64 app servers
a.html: fun claim(handle: String, userId: String): Boolean { val holders = jdbc.queryForList( "SELECT user_id FROM handles WHERE name = ?", String::class.java, handle) if (holders.isNotEmpty()) return false // another server can run the same SELECT right here, and see no row either jdbc.update("INSERT INTO handles (name, user_id) VALUES (?, ?)", handle, userId) return true }

b.label: A log keyed by the handle
b.title: the client side
b.html: fun claim(handle: String, userId: String): Decision { val requestId = UUID.randomUUID().toString() // kept across retries of this claim val record = ProducerRecord("handle-claims", handle, Claim(requestId, userId, handle)) producer.send(record).get() // key = handle: one partition decides // a consumer of "handle-decisions" completes one future per request id return pending.getOrPut(requestId) { CompletableFuture() }.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

compare.note: The first version decides in 64 places at once and hopes the SELECT and the INSERT of two servers never interleave. The second decides in exactly one place per handle: the processor of the partition the key hashes to. It pays for that with a trip through the log and a wait for the reply, the timeliness cost, and it needs the request ID so a retried send can't count as a second claim. In a single database, a unique index with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is the same idea with the database as the one decider.

lab.title: Unique handles and cross-partition transfers, without coordination
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. 19 tests run and 18 fail with NotImplementedError. The one that passes is the race: checkThenInsert is finished, and it grants handles twice. Scheduler.kt is finished too: it runs tasks in a seeded random order, so every count is exact.
In Claims.kt, write partitionFor. Then write ClaimProcessor.decide: you need a map from handle to owner and a map from request ID to the decision already given. Run ClaimsTest.
Read throughLog (finished) and find the one line that picks a partition. The test keyed by userId instead... passes a different key function to your own code. Watch it grant duplicates.

In Transfers.kt, write WalletProcessor.handle. The KDoc lists three cases for a request and one for a credit. Run TransfersTest; assertIntegrity at the bottom of the file lists exactly what must hold after crashes, replays and client retries. When everything passes, delete the duplicate check for credits and run TransfersTest again. Which tests fail, and which line of assertIntegrity catches it first?
hints: decide: return decided[claim.requestId] if it's there. Otherwise grant when the holder is null or is the same user, reject otherwise, and store the decision under the request ID before you return it.
handle for a Requested: look in outcomes first and reply with what you find. Only debit and call send when balances.getValue(t.from) covers the amount, and record the outcome either way.
handle for a Credit: creditsApplied.add(msg.requestId) returns false if the ID was already there; return early in that case.

drill.title: Constraints through a log, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) write partitionFor and the decision rule for one claim, in about six lines; (2) list the four things that make the cross-partition transfer safe; (3) define timeliness and integrity in one sentence each, with one example violation of each; (4) name two rules that are not invariant confluent.

answer.html:
(1) partitionFor(key, n) = Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), n)
    decide(c): if c.requestId was answered, return that answer
               holder = owner[c.username]
               if holder == null or holder == c.userId: owner[c.username] = c.userId; Granted
               else Rejected(held by holder); remember the answer under c.requestId
(2) order within each partition; at-least-once delivery;
    processors whose decisions depend only on what they read;
    one request id from the client to the last write, checked at every consumer
(3) timeliness: users see up-to-date state; violation: a stale read that fixes
    itself (the credit shows up 200 ms later)
    integrity: nothing lost, invented or contradictory; violation: permanent
    (a credit applied twice stays applied twice)
(4) uniqueness of a value the user chooses; a counter with a lower bound under
    decrements (balance >= 0); also foreign-key deletes and sequential IDs

recap: A uniqueness rule needs one decider per value. Send every claim for a value to one log partition, keyed by that value, and let one single-threaded processor decide in log order.
The partition key is the constraint: key by anything other than the constrained value and two processors can each say yes, silently.

A transfer across partitions needs no distributed transaction. One appended request is the atomic step; the debit and the credit are derived from it by processors that decide only from what they read and drop duplicates by request ID.

Timeliness violations (stale reads) heal when you wait; integrity violations (lost, duplicated or contradictory data) are permanent. Guarantee integrity everywhere and buy timeliness only where a user needs it.

Many rules can be checked late and repaired with an apology. Invariant confluence says which can't: a unique value the user chooses, and a balance that must stay above zero, need one decider; most other rules don't.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Logs can't enforce constraints. If we want unique handles we need a distributed lock or a database." Explain how a partitioned log enforces uniqueness, what it costs, and the one mistake that breaks it.
explain.answer: Uniqueness needs one decider per value, not a database. If every claim for a handle is keyed by that handle, all of them land in one partition, and one single-threaded processor reads that partition in order. It keeps a table of taken handles, grants the first claim for each handle in log order and rejects the rest, and remembers each request ID so a redelivered claim gets the same answer. Its state comes only from the partition, so after a crash it replays and decides the same way. Claims for different handles go to different partitions and are decided in parallel, so it scales by adding partitions. The cost is timeliness: the client must append and then wait for the decision to come back, so a claim is a round trip through the log. The mistake that breaks it is keying by anything other than the handle, such as the user ID. Then two claims for the same handle reach two processors with separate tables, and both are granted, without any error.

deeper.html:
Splitting a budget. A daily payout limit of 10,000.00 per merchant is a counter with an upper bound, so two regions can't each check it alone. They can if you split it: give each region 5,000.00 to spend without asking, and let a region that runs low ask the other for part of its share. Building on Quicksand discusses escrow locking, a related scheme for commutative operations such as addition and subtraction, and the CRDT literature calls the replicated form a bounded counter. The trade is plain: no coordination on the common path, a little on the rare one.

Reading is not deciding. A sign-up form that shows "@ana is available" as you type is reading a derived view, and it may be stale. That's fine, as long as the claim itself goes through the processor and the user is told the real answer. Treat every check made outside the decider as a hint for the user interface, never as the decision.

Where the order runs out. One partition orders the claims for one handle. Nothing orders a claim on partition 0 against a transfer on partition 3, and rules that relate records in different partitions ("a user may hold at most three handles") need those records routed together, or a second step that checks and repairs. Lesson 1 showed where a single total order stops; past that point, order per key is all you get.

The username-claim and multi-partition payment designs are discussed in Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 13, which builds on the online event processing paper cited above.
